Patient Vignette: Mrs. A.

Mrs. A. is an 80-year-old woman of Oceania descent, who has been married for fifty-two years. She presents as a solid, sturdy woman, her hands calloused and scarred from a lifetime of work. She speaks with a measured, deliberate tone, often pausing to look down at her lap before continuing. She has been a welder for over forty years, a trade she learned from her father as a young woman in the islands. She still works part-time at a small fabrication shop, finding comfort in the familiar hiss and flash of the arc welder.

The trauma she describes began early in her marriage, though she is careful to frame it as something that "just happened" at first. Her husband, a fisherman, had a temper that would flare without warning. The first time he hit her was over a meal she had burned. She was twenty-eight, pregnant with their second child. She remembers the shock more than the pain—the way the room tilted, the sound of her own gasp. She did not tell anyone. In her community, marriage was sacred, and a wife’s duty was to endure.

Over the next two decades, the abuse became a rhythm. It was not constant, but it was predictable. It would follow a pattern: a tense silence, a minor provocation, then the explosion. He never hit her face, always her body—her ribs, her back, her arms. She learned to stand still and take it, to keep her hands at her sides so he could not accuse her of fighting back. She wore long-sleeved shirts, even in the tropical heat. At the welding shop, she found a strange sanctuary. The mask protected her face. The noise of the grinder and the torch drowned out the sound of her own thoughts. The physical demands of the work—lifting heavy steel, holding a position for hours—made her body strong, but it also made the bruises easier to explain. "Fell off a ladder," she would say. "Dropped a beam on my arm."

The abuse stopped about fifteen years ago, when her husband’s health declined. He is now frail, dependent on her for care. She feeds him, bathes him, dresses his wounds. She does this without malice, but also without tenderness. She says she is "just doing what needs to be done."

In the past year, since she turned eighty, Mrs. A. has noticed a change in herself. She cannot sleep. Not the kind of insomnia where she lies awake worrying—she simply cannot stay in bed. She gets up at two or three in the morning and goes to her workshop in the garage. She lights the torch and welds scrap metal together, creating small, abstract shapes. She does not know what she is making. She just needs the light, the heat, the concentration.

During the day, she is easily startled. A car backfiring on the street makes her drop whatever she is holding. Her husband’s voice, calling her from another room, makes her heart pound so hard she feels dizzy. She has started checking the locks on the doors repeatedly, even though she knows no one is coming. She avoids the kitchen when the stove is on, because the smell of burning food makes her nauseous. She cannot remember the last time she cooked a meal.

She tells me these things without emotion, as if describing a machine that is malfunctioning. She does not say she is afraid. She says she is "on edge." She does not say she is sad. She says she is "tired." When I ask her about the past, she looks at me with a flat, steady gaze and says, "That was a long time ago. I don’t think about it." But her hands, resting on her knees, are trembling.
